A precise understanding of $B_s^0$ meson lifetimes holds significant value in identifying the fundamental processes governing the decay of heavy quarks and can reveal the existence of unknown particles beyond the Standard Model. The LHCb collaboration leverages two distinct decay channels to enhance the statistical precision of the $B_s^0$ lifetime measurement. Furthermore, this analysis utilizes shape parameters derived from shape models and sidebands in order to mitigate biases stemming from the presence of other particles. The latest measurement yields a $B_s^0$ lifetime of 1.408 picoseconds with a corresponding uncertainty of 0.011 picoseconds.

This study addresses a key challenge in solving the value function of an optimal control problem with rough data. We develop an algorithm that modifies a classical policy iteration method, specifically tailored to the discrete version of the value function. The policy iteration framework is applied using mild evaluations and aggressive interpolations, and we establish the algorithm's convergence. The method is seen as a numerical solution technique, and an connection to the full-fractional dynamic programming equation is confirmed through discretization. Notably, convergence is achieved in the $C^{1,\gamma}$ norm, overcoming limitations of prior work limited to $C^{0,\gamma}$ data.

Our analysis of dipole anisotropy in the cosmic ray direction focuses on very high-energy particles in the sky map created by the Pierre Auger Observatory. We examine the size of the dipole moment as a function of energy, separating data into energy bins, and also explore the dependence of the dipole moment on other parameters like maximum linear dimension and energy spectrum. We compare our findings to simulations without magnetic field influence, revealing a slight increase in the dipole moment with energy, which is statistically insignificant. We also observe that the findings are consistent with the assumed LHC energy spectrum and linearly related to the energy spectrum parameter $\delta$. Our study also indicates that the observed data is not significantly influenced by the linearly related large scale component in the direction map.

In this study, the interplay between the centrality of collisions and the
alteration of the nuclear modification factor $R_{p p}^{A A}$ as a function of
transverse momentum $p_{T}$ in heavy-ion collisions is investigated within the
framework of the parton energy loss model. To address the varying degrees of
freezing out in various systems, a common phase boundary in the $T-\tau$ plane
is employed to determine the final momentum of partons. Calculated results for
lead-lead and proton-lead collisions at the LHC and a limited set of results
for lead-lead collisions in a more detailed analysis demonstrate that the
nuclear modification factor $R_{p p}^{A A}$ exhibits a direct correlation with
the centrality of collisions and a given transverse momentum, with highly
central collisions characterized by larger energy loss and a higher freeze-out
temperature.

The equivalence of two formulations in noncommutative quantum mechanics has been demonstrated, specifically the relationship between the standard approach using noncommuting coordinates and the phase-space formulation featuring a commuting momentum space. Through the Weyl-Wigner transform, the matrix mechanics approach was derived from the coordinate-based formulation. Similarly, the Heisenberg picture was obtained in the phase-space formulation with explicitly computed noncommutative analogs for the Heisenberg equations of motion.

The primary objective of this research is to assess the effectiveness of deep learning techniques in identifying tumor infiltrating lymphocytes within digitized histological tissue samples. The dataset used for testing consists of 100 randomly selected tissue samples, which were manually annotated to enhance the accuracy of the models. We tested two deep learning models, Mask R-CNN and Faster R-CNN, which were trained to detect and classify lymphocytes in the images. The results indicated that the Mask R-CNN model outperformed the Faster R-CNN model with an accuracy of 85% compared to 75%. The data used for training and testing was collected from 200 and 100 randomly selected images, respectively.

This paper proposes an enhanced version of the WDFE algorithm, termed J-WDFE, by integrating it with the MLSE algorithm, resulting in a algorithm capable of correcting multiple-symbol errors. The new algorithm is applied to systems with time-varying impairments, which include fiber-optic communication systems. A simulation is conducted to demonstrate the efficacy of the J-WDFE algorithm in terms of reducing errors, particularly when dealing with burst errors, fiber-optic communication systems, and systems with constant impairments.

Deep learning models have achieved remarkable success in computer vision tasks, but their large size and high memory requirements often limit their use in resource-constrained environments. To address this issue, researchers have been working on developing more efficient models. However, the complex interplay between model architecture and performance makes it difficult to find the optimal design. In this paper, we introduce an automatic dilation optimizer (ADO) that can efficiently explore the vast space of valid Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN) architectures to find the most efficient one. By using a bi-level optimization process, ADO iteratively refines the dilation configuration of each layer to minimize model size while maintaining acceptable performance. Our method is unique in that it is the first to automatically optimize a TCN's dilation structure. We demonstrate the effectiveness of ADO on multiple datasets, including ImageNet and CIFAR-100, and show that it can produce highly efficient models with up to 10x reduced model size and 1.5x lower inference latency compared to manually designed models. Furthermore, ADO is a general framework that can be applied to other types of networks.

This paper provides a comprehensive examination of the properties of finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebras, revealing their ability to be decomposed into direct sums of indecomposable components. Our investigation reveals that the nilpotency and solvability dimensions of Zinbiel algebras are directly linked to those of their associated Lie admissible algebras. Additionally, we establish upper-bound formulas for the lower central series terms of a Zinbiel algebra based on its dimension. A key finding is that the Zinbiel lower central series terms mirror the structure of their Admissible Lie counterparts. Moreover, this research reveals that the nilpotency and solvability dimensions of a direct sum algebra are determined by the corresponding dimensions of its indecomposable components. Finally, several examples are provided to illustrate the diversity in nilpotency and solvability dimensions among Zinbiel algebras of dimension four.

The connection between flow fluctuations in particle number and flow asymmetries in transverse direction observed in particle spectra from heavy-ion collisions at the LHC and RHIC suggests that quark-gluon plasma flow characteristics significantly reflect the initial geometric fluctuations of the collision. Notably, flow fluctuations are not directly correlated with higher-order momentum moments, indicating that viscous effects do not interfere with this correlation. A quantitative model based on hydrodynamics successfully replicates the fluctuation measurements found in particle number and flow asymmetries from Pb-Pb collisions at 2.76 TeV, confirming that flow variations are primarily influenced by initial geometric fluctuations with only minor adjustments due to hydrodynamic dynamics.

We extend our previous work on computing first-order correspondents in complex modal logic formulas by examining ALBA's role in the computation process for (D)LE-formulas. Our approach builds upon the algorithmic framework developed in prior studies, incorporating 'bunched assertions' to expand the modal grammar. This results in a broader grammar that includes diamonds, boxes, negations, and classical connectives. By applying our revised ALBA algorithm, we can derive explicit first-order correspondents for HCLQ formulas, including double negations. Furthermore, the ALBA computation process provides insights into the existence of PDLQ definability by offering both a positive and negative first-order counterpart, potentially based on the quantificational depth of existential and universal first-order correspondents.

This paper explores first-order logic within the four-valued Lukasiewicz framework, specifically focusing on query evaluation and assertion in contexts where truth values extend beyond traditional binary understanding. We specifically investigate the impact of treating database views as defined by stable models in datalog programs, and demonstrate that queries can be effectively answered using four-valued logic when these views are incorporated. Our analysis reveals that answering certain types of queries, particularly conjunctive queries, remains computationally feasible within these expanded logic frameworks. We also propose a novel approach to consistent query answering, utilizing the framework of four-valued logic to account for potential contradictions in database information. This approach allows us to determine whether there exists a reliable interpretation of the database that satisfies a given set of constraints and yields a specific query result. Our findings indicate that this method of consistent query answering is computationally efficient and can be achieved through the use of database repairs that extend the original database with view stability conditions.

This paper introduces a novel non-stationary time series model, the Time-Varying Poisson AutoRegressive with exogenous covariates (TV-PARX) model, to address complex nonlinear dynamics and sudden shifts in data structures. We propose a flexible TV-PARX model that accommodates these challenges, and we develop an efficient parameter estimation method using the Empirical Bayes approach. To assess the model's performance, we utilize a leave-one-out cross-validation method for hyperparameter optimization. We employ a semi-parametric smoothing technique to estimate time-varying coefficients and their confidence intervals. Our results, obtained through Monte Carlo simulations and real-world data analysis, demonstrate the superiority of the TV-PARX model over existing models in terms of forecasting accuracy.

I have developed Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs), a novel framework for learning tactile object descriptions in 3D environments. NDFs map object descriptions to neural features, which are then used to input into a neural network that predicts actions. By learning this process from data, both single and multiple demonstrations, NDFs can learn manipulation tasks. Notably, this approach is efficient, requiring minimal computation during actual use. NDFs are particularly effective at learning from limited demonstrations because they learn a low-dimensional neural feature space that generalizes across various viewpoints and locations. This is demonstrated by evaluating NDFs on the Tactile Flow dataset, where NDFs are shown to be an efficient and robust approach to learning manipulation from limited demonstrations.

The SiD Detector, which is being designed for the upgraded CLIC ILD detector at the International Linear Collider, will ensure precise tracking of particles and accurate measurement of their energies. Its calorimeter system will consist of two components: a high-granularity calorimeter and a standard calorimeter. A simulation of the detector's performance at a 500 GeV center-of-mass energy, accounting for hadronization effects, will be compared to pure particle flow algorithms. The simulation of hadronization effects involves applying corrections to the reconstructed energy and applying a correction to the resolution. The result is a pure algorithm with a relative resolution of 0.7% at 100 GeV and 1.0% at 1,000 GeV for single jets along the z-axis.

We've obtained high-resolution spectra for 15 blue horizontal branch stars in the globular cluster Tononzintla 2, which has a high metal content. By analyzing these spectra, we found that the spread in the abundance of various chemical elements is unusually large, especially for iron, which is atypical for a high-metallicity cluster. Furthermore, the spectra indicate the presence of distinct populations with different compositions, which is consistent with previous studies of other galaxies. A particular star, designated T2-10, has an extremely high iron content compared to the rest of the cluster, which is an extreme outlier. These findings highlight the need for more in-depth research to better understand the nature of chemical variations in this galaxy.

The arXiv and similar resources for research previews feature link analysis that reveals their scale-free nature, with the node in-degree distribution's exponent reflecting the depth of connections. In contrast, the GitHub repository for formal proof demonstrations in computer science shows a smaller exponent in-degree distribution, with some research areas exhibiting higher connectivity. The arXiv's structure primarily reflects research dependencies, whereas the GitHub repository's connectivity is influenced by shared build frameworks and duplicated code. Furthermore, both the arXiv and GitHub repository's out-degree distributions follow power laws, indicating that a minority of research topics and software projects have a significant impact on their respective fields.

A reanalysis of the Borel singularity position from our earlier study, "Conformal Window of QCD in Three Dimensions Revisited" has been conducted with additional data, resulting in a more accurate estimate. The revised calculation yields a critical Borel singularity value of |z_c| between 11.5 and 13.5 times the heavy quark mass, particularly for systems with four or fewer light quarks. The lower bound of 11.5 is derived from the most stringent input parameters, particularly in lattice spacing and quark mass determinations. The discrepancy between the critical singularity location and the pQCD expansion endpoint for systems with two light quarks suggests that perturbative reliability may be maintained in the four-quark sector, potentially resolving concerns regarding color-anti-quark meson stability. The phase transition between confined and Coulombic regimes is estimated to occur near systems with two heavy and four light quarks, marking a shift from confinement to a Coulombic regime. The reliance on lattice parameters for this estimate is minimal, primarily determined by the conformal ratio z_0. The calculation of the critical singularity location is further complicated by the presence of non-holographic poles in the fundamental correlator, necessitating a detailed analysis of their impact on the critical ratio. The calculation of these pole contributions is performed for select systems, with the most significant contribution found in the four-quark sector, reducing the critical ratio to approximately

We investigate the relationship between the thermodynamics of the Talagancer's asymmetric-planted model and the performance of the approximate message-passing algorithm when solving the $\mathbb{Z}_2$-synchronization problem. Our study specifically focuses on the odd-degree Cayley tree. By examining a particular class of potentials, including the logarithmic potential, we demonstrate that the TAP free energy and the APP free energy exhibit equivalent values, and that the approximate message-passing algorithm converges to the global minimum of the free energy landscape. Our findings also extend to the case of the BPS function, where the equivalence holds despite the potential being non-logarithmic.

Generalized Sheet Transition Conditions form the basis for creating advanced metasurfaces, which are then used to manipulate electromagnetic waves in various ways. This paper presents a novel approach to developing efficient and versatile methods for designing metasurfaces capable of controlling the scattering of complex objects. Our proposed method incorporates the implicit relationship between surface currents and electromagnetic wave scattering to establish a clear and effective design framework. This framework enables the creation of sophisticated metasurfaces with high accuracy and ease of use. Our method has been successfully applied to achieve several objectives, including the accurate scattering control of aircraft models, enhanced radar cross-section performance, and radar cross-section reduction of complex objects. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in achieving these objectives with high precision and minimal computational resources.

In this study, we successfully applied a modified blowing-up technique to two types of linearizable orbits, specifically those with orbital contact and the orbit of infinity in a near-Hamiltonian system. By leveraging this method, we were able to obtain new, more general linearization results for orbits with varying degrees of complexity. Furthermore, we identified conditions under which linearization can be achieved in a neighborhood of infinity.

A new deep learning model, the electron-correlation perceptron (eCPNN), has been proposed, which builds a flexible function representation based on John Hopfield networks and employs electron pair distances as inputs to generate potential functions. The eCPNN's potential functions are then used in a many-body trial wave function to calculate energy through a Monte Carlo integration method. When applied to the helium ground state within a Coulomb interaction framework, the eCPNN model achieved a highly accurate total energy calculation of -2.90355, closely matching the exact result of -2.90372. Furthermore, the model demonstrated superior performance in describing electron density and electron-electron correlation when compared to traditional B-spline methods. Notably, the model exhibited an impressive ability to capture the correct cusp behavior at zero-distance electron interactions.

Recent observations from the Dark Energy Camera's DECaLS survey have uncovered a massive arc-like structure in the sky, potentially a new class of cosmic formation. By analyzing redshifted galaxy images, researchers have identified a large arc formed by galaxies at a specific distance from Earth, which is about 1.5 billion parsecs across. The arc is situated 1.2 billion parsecs away and is centered in a part of the sky not covered by previous studies. The arc's shape and location are unlikely to be a result of survey bias, and its existence challenges the standard model of the universe's formation. The findings suggest that more data is needed to confirm the arc's existence and to understand its implications for the cosmic web.

A new strategy for determining the day sky brightness over a wide area is proposed, with optical depth maps created for the aerosols in the atmosphere. This approach uses wide-field photometry to measure the color of the sky, which can then be used to determine the optical depth of the aerosols without the need for precise calibration of the equipment. This was tested with a portable device that scanned the sky in the north direction, and the results were compared to established models of the sky. While the results showed good agreement with the data obtained from the device, some discrepancies were noted, which may be attributed to the limitations of the equipment and the complexity of the atmosphere. With some improvements to the device, this strategy could be used to create real-time maps of the atmosphere over a wide area, which could be useful for monitoring volcanic eruptions and forest fires.

Estimating the pose of objects in complex scenes is a challenging task. Our proposed method leverages projection grouping, an extension of the well-known reprojection error, to handle difficult object poses. By analyzing the relationships between projected object components, our neural network learns to infer their spatial configuration. Our approach yields superior results on the IMU dataset and the AIST++ dataset, particularly in object pose estimation, and on two projection grouping tasks.

Peridynamic theories rely heavily on kernel structure, which significantly influences the model's ability to predict failures. However, there is a lack of research focusing on how to select appropriate kernels. This study bridges this gap by exploring the impact of kernel variations on predictions of material damage. Utilizing a simple model, we investigate the peridynamic response to tension and explore the conditions under which cracks form. Our analysis reveals that crack prediction is influenced by the distribution of material interactions, which can be examined through a critical threshold in these interactions. This exploration provides a foundation for systematically evaluating and choosing peridynamic kernels that accurately reflect real-world materials.

We extend Graphical Lasso (Greedy Maximum Likelihood Estimation for Gaussian Models) to incorporate unseen variables, creating a new statistical framework. This enhancement allows the model to capture complex relationships, including higher-order correlations, by implicitly modeling additional source variables. As a result, it becomes computationally challenging, resembling an enhanced version of Graphical Lasso. We devise an efficient, scalable algorithm to solve this model, creating a series of simpler sub-problems that can be solved quickly. This leads to a solution converging to a stationary point. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through various synthetic data experiments, showing its ability to efficiently model latent variables and provide accurate estimates.

To evaluate the effectiveness of esmgrid on diverse computational tasks, we conducted a benchmark test using the alanine dipeptide system. The test compared esmgrid against JAX using identical simulation code. The results indicated that for smaller systems, esmgrid provided a 2x speedup over pure JAX, while for more complex systems, esmgrid delivered an order of magnitude speedup. The speedup increased with the size of the integrator step size and the length of the simulated trajectory. The advantages of esmgrid were further highlighted by its compatibility with multi-GPU and multi-node distributed computing, offering both greater flexibility and scalability.

This study investigates how binary black holes interact with their surrounding, self-gravitating disks of dark matter, focusing on the influence of this interaction on the binary's movement and the resulting gravitational waves. A numerical method, combining N-body and mesh-gravity techniques, was used to simulate these interactions. The results show that the binary's movement is primarily determined by general relativistic effects at close range, while the disk's influence is dominant at a greater distance. Notably, the disk can induce long-lasting, complex movements in the binary, causing it to occasionally return to the disk's dominant region of influence. The outcome of this process depends on the disk's initial state and can result in either the binary merging or being ejected from the system. This interaction can also lead to the formation of stable, central orbits, surrounded by more chaotic, outer orbits.

This paper investigates the long-term behavior of a damped dynamic system defined on a star-shaped graph with complex, asymmetric elasticity in its transverse direction. As elasticity varies along the graph's edges, we demonstrate that the system's exponential stability is sensitive to the elasticity's properties. Our analysis reveals that under specific conditions, the system achieves optimal stability based on the minimum elasticity, whereas other conditions lead to suboptimal or absent stability, illustrating the graph's geometry's significant impact on the damping effect.

Researchers are studying the effects of Stycast 1090SI, a transparent epoxy used in various applications, on acoustic waves.  By creating flat samples of varying thicknesses, the study found that the acoustic properties of Stycast are similar to those of PMMA, a common material used in acoustics.  Specifically, the impedance of Stycast is 1.5 times that of PMMA, while the attenuation of Stycast is 1.5 times lower than PMMA.  The experimental results confirmed the theoretical predictions made by the Kramers-Kronig relations.  However, the study also identified the effects of surface reflections, which can distort the results.  To address this, the researchers developed a formula to correct the results and accurately determine the attenuation and real part of the impedance of Stycast.  The corrected results showed that the attenuation of the material is 0.5dB/cm at 50kHz, 2.0dB/cm at 200kHz, and 8.0dB/cm at 800kHz.

The structure of most real-world networks involves multiple layers, where the connections between nodes can vary both within and across layers. To accurately assess the significance of nodes in these multi-layer networks, it's crucial to account for the inter-layer relationships, often referred to as topological equivalence. This study introduces a novel betweenness centrality measure for computing the betweenness centrality of nodes in multi-layer networks, taking into consideration the topological equivalence of nodes. It also conducts numerical experiments to demonstrate the effectiveness of our algorithm in terms of both performance and centrist qualities. Furthermore, it is shown that our inter-layer constraints significantly enhance the computational centerality of nodes, particularly in networks composed of numerous layers.

This research focuses on developing a deconvolution method to enhance the clarity of blurred images captured by a camera. The study addresses the issue of color dependency in point spread functions and proposes a method to account for this effect. A new approach is introduced to model the camera system, which includes the introduction of a color-independent deconvolution method. The results of the proposed system and the traditional white light deconvolution are compared, demonstrating the benefits of the new color-dependent approach. The outcomes indicate a significant reduction in the full width at half maximum error when using the new method, and the improved performance of the camera system is showcased through the comparison of the two approaches.

A novel global coordinate system has been established for the R-Minkowski spacetime, which utilizes de Sitter spacetime as a coordinate framework. In this coordinate framework, the Dirac equation was solved within the R-Minkowski spacetime, yielding a complete set of Dirac plane waves that can be expressed in terms of de Sitter spacetime. The relationship between the two spacetimes was further explored by examining how the Diric equation behaves under conformal transformation, which led to a direct connection between the Dirac equation in the R-Minkowski spacetime and the de Sitter spacetime. As a result, the de Sitter spacetime Dirac equation was derived from its Minkowski spacetime counterpart. The transformation of the de Sitter spacetime Dirac equation into the R-Minkowski spacetime allows for a novel interpretation of the de Sitter spacetime Dirac equation, which can be viewed as a restricted form of the R-Minkowski spacetime Dirac equation.

We present the Causal Graph Modeling approach, a method for constructing and assessing probabilistic models that capture the causes and effects of events within a specific domain. This approach is detailed in the documentation of the 'cdt' package, a Python package developed to facilitate this type of modeling. The documentation can be accessed at the given URL. The approach is based on a refined version of the Causal Graph Model, a theory that models events as a combination of independent components, where the components' effects determine a joint distribution. By representing events as combinations of their components, the refined version allows for a more detailed and detailed analysis of complex systems. The 'cdt' package implements this refined version, including the integration of temporal and spatial aspects, to efficiently model and analyze data. The package provides a range of tools for compiling, decomposing, and evaluating graphs, as well as for optimizing graphs for inference. The source code and documentation for the 'cdt' package are available at the given URL.

A novel seal design featuring a central cavity with an orifice is introduced to delay the failure of hydraulic piston systems by mitigating the impact force. The cavity's pressure drop triggers the formation of a mixing layer and potential cavity collapse, which can be influenced by the orifice size and impact velocity. High-speed imaging reveals that increased impact velocities result in more pronounced surface oscillations of the seal, while pressure reductions within the cavity deepen and accelerate the rate at which they occur. Smaller orifice sizes lead to deeper pressure reductions, whereas larger orifice sizes generate vortex rings that maintain the cavity's stability. The design effectively mitigates impact forces, reducing the acceleration experienced by the piston by a factor of 100.

Using string field theory, we explore the relationship between the Witten effect's generalized form and the spectrum of charged quantum gravity states. By applying light-cone gauge, we find that adding a negative charge to an extremal Reissner-Nordstr\"om black hole reveals an infinite series of charged state states in the quantum gravity spectrum, which correspond to the F1 D-brane states.

Mobile applications are frequently targeted by malicious actors, and while static analysis has been extensively studied, effective static analysis tools for Android apps are still in short supply. The development of a novel static analysis framework called OctopOS is introduced, which was designed to pinpoint vulnerable code within Android applications susceptible to common security threats. The OctopOS framework was successfully tested on a large dataset of 10,000 real-world apps from Google Play, where it pinpointed 6,900 apps containing at least one vulnerability. The octopOS framework was also evaluated for its precision, and the results showed that the octopOS was capable of pinpointing 91.5 percent of manually confirmed security flaws. The source code for octopOS is freely accessible on GitHub.

We examine the FPG algorithm within the context of episodic controlled Markov
systems with bounded stochastic disturbances and limited observations. We present a
doubly linear sample complexity achievement policy learning algorithm under the
assumption of a gap between eigenvalues that is polynomially related to the
gap between the nearest and furthest points. Our analysis shows that even when a
substantial portion of episodes are intentionally disrupted, the policy's learning
process remains unaffected due to the filtering process of the FPG algorithm.

A solution to the original paradox of the "Three Card Game" proposed by Martin Gardner in 1968 is presented, which relies on a fundamental mathematical concept - element of choice. The author argues that without the ability to make a specific choice, players are unable to gain an advantage over one another. The paper critiques several alternative solutions and presents a straightforward solution to the paradox based on the selection of a specific element. The author also presents a modified version of the game with multiple rounds and proves that this variation can be won by the player with the ability to make a choice, yielding a superior outcome compared to the original game's zero-sum result.

First ab initio calculations provide a comprehensive explanation for the cubanite's remarkable physical properties, including its chemical resilience, ferromagnetic behavior, charge stability, and unique optical characteristics. Furthermore, our study of the electron-phonon interaction using a model based on linearized spectral functions yields the cubanite's phonon spectrum and its scattering rates for electrons. By comparing the calculated results with experimental data, we are able to pinpoint the origin of the cubanite's distinct optical absorption features.

The study proposes a novel approach to all-electric control of quantum dot-acoustic cavity interactions through frequency adjustment of a driving laser. Rabi oscillations can be modulated by changing the frequency of the driving laser, allowing for precise tuning of the quantum dot's frequency. A quantum state transfer protocol is also presented, utilizing this all-electric frequency transfer method.

A theoretical framework for a herringbone lattice Hamiltonian is established, 
incorporating on-site potential asymmetry, nearest-neighbor hopping asymmetry, 
and a unit cell magnetic flux. By adjusting these parameters, the lattice exhibits 
either time-reversal symmetric or broken symmetry, which can be further modified 
through perturbation of the Hamiltonian. An analytical method is used to determine 
the energy spectrum and wave functions of the lattice, allowing for an examination 
of its topological properties. The study reveals the presence of Chern numbers in 
both non-Abelian and diagonal forms, and the modification of the Chern number can 
be achieved by changing the parameters of the lattice. The research also explores 
the effects of introducing a magnetic flux into the lattice, and the modification 
of its properties can be achieved by adjusting the flux.

Researchers have been exploring the potential of single-photon catalyzed coherent states (SPCCSs) for their use in continuous-variable quantum communication, teleportation, and computation. Interestingly, the process of generating SPCCSs can result in the creation of not only desired states containing one added photon but also unwanted states with multiple added photons. In this research, we examine the likelihood of successfully generating SPCCSs through two distinct methods: using beam splitters and parametric amplifiers. The studies show that the success probabilities for these two approaches differ significantly. Specifically, when using beam splitters, the probability of successfully generating SPCCSs is the square of the probability observed when using parametric amplifiers. This research also investigates how the success probabilities are influenced by the catalytic photons and compares the findings with previously reported results.
The provided summary can be found in the following source: 10.1143/CTP.888.1.

A significant challenge in protein engineering lies in the difficulty of pinpointing the natural variations found within a protein family. This issue is compounded by the vast amount of sequence data that needs to be processed. We introduce a novel approach to learning the rules governing protein polymers, based on inferring a generative model that captures natural variations within protein families. This model, which operates as a Bernoulli factor graph, allows for the efficient processing of large datasets using a stochastic gradient method. Notably, it can handle the entire corpus of protein sequences available on the web. Our approach yields a compact representation of each protein, where each protein is seen as a combination of independent components, each component corresponding to a specific sequence position. This representation, which has been shown to outperform existing methods in various benchmarks, is now being applied to predict sequence functionality and is available for public use.

A novel ventilator setup is proposed, involving one central machine that can fully or partially ventilate up to two individuals. In this arrangement, one set of ventilator tubes remains closed during ventilation of a single patient. When a second patient needs assistance, a valve redirects airflow from the primary set of tubes to the secondary tube. When both patients need full ventilatory support, a second valve from the secondary set of tubes is activated to draw in additional airflow from the second machine. This setup allows for one machine to fully ventilate a second patient while simultaneously providing partial support to a third patient on the primary set of tubes. Notably, each patient receives their own unique, tailored level of ventilatory support.

A critical medical task that demands high precision and a significant amount of time is the segmentation of the esophagus.  To address this challenge, a deep learning model called "Dilated Dense Attention Unet" has been developed to enhance the precision of automatic segmentation of the esophagus.  This innovative network integrates two key components: Dense Blocks that facilitate feature reuse and long-range dependency modeling, and an Attention Unet that refines the segmentation process by emphasizing relevant features.  To optimize the model's performance, a two-stage training strategy has been employed, which initially focuses on low-level feature extraction and subsequently refines the segmentation by leveraging dense features.  Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed model outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in terms of segmentation accuracy.  The model's efficacy has been validated through comprehensive evaluations on the esophagus segmentation dataset.  The dataset and evaluation results are available online at https://github.com/zhengzhengzheng/DAUNet.

This paper introduces a novel approach, form-eval-lm, leveraging a trained language model to streamline the formation evaluation process using acoustic logs. By streamlining the evaluation, the new method allows for real-time application on a rig, reducing the time and resources required. To achieve this, we incorporate Acoustic Impedance Range Mapping (AIRM) and Acoustic Impedance Range Mapping Limit (ARML) concepts into the evaluation process, which narrows the range of possible outcomes and significantly reduces the probability of errors. To further refine the evaluation, we develop an algorithm, LM-EnRML, that integrates the AIRM and ARML constraints into the language model, which assigns a more accurate score to the correct formation evaluation. The proposed form-eval-lm method and LM-EnRML algorithm were tested on a comprehensive dataset comprising 10,000 well logs, and the results showed that the approach achieved a high accuracy rate of 93.5% and an F1-score of 0.87.

Named entity recognition (NER) is a fundamental task in natural language processing, and this study explores the effectiveness of using linear attention memory networks (LAMMs) for this task. Our LAMMs models are capable of integrating external knowledge, specifically corpus-level information, to capture long-distance dependencies in text. By incorporating LAMMs into the NER pipeline, our research shows a notable improvement in NER performance. Furthermore, our experiments on the LAMM architecture reveal its adaptability and potential for enhancing other NLP tasks through the injection of corpus-level information. To validate our findings, we LAMMs are used for part-of-speech tagging and semantic role labeling, resulting in a small but significant improvement in performance.

We analyze the rationality of bitangents in a specific quartic curve within a uniquely structured region of its parameter space. This region is defined by the boundaries of edges in a related graph, and we examine how bitangents behave as we traverse inside this region, influenced by a twist along each edge. Our analysis reveals that the rationality of these bitangents is determined by an odd parity condition, and we calculate this parity for each edge, ultimately revealing that the rationality of these bitangents is intimately connected to a change in monodromy, and that edges with this specific parity are those where the bitangent becomes non-trivial.

This research focuses on developing a high-precision algorithm to track the movement of mobile targets using only passive acoustic source detection. To test the algorithm's performance, its effectiveness was validated through field experiments and compared to idealized simulation data. The results showed that the algorithm can accurately track targets with minimal error, confirming its effectiveness. Specifically, the algorithm achieved an average error of 1.09 meters, which is very close to the simulation's average error of 0.94 meters. Additionally, it successfully tracked the movement of a moving target with 100% accuracy, demonstrating its capability to track mobile objects. The research also compared the algorithm's performance to existing methods, revealing that it outperforms traditional and advanced approaches in terms of precision.

The rapid growth of global multilingualism has made technology that processes and understands human language vital for multiple languages. Building on this, the advancement of computing has made it possible for researchers to develop sophisticated natural language models, with significant research implications that span across various fields. By examining the progress of NLP research, we can identify its potential to positively impact society through multilingualism in areas such as education, public services, and media, while also highlighting the challenges that need to be addressed to overcome data scarcity for underrepresented languages and ensure equal access to computational resources.

A significant number of images shared on social media platforms lack descriptions, which is a major issue for visually impaired users trying to engage with these platforms. Although image captioning technology has seen substantial progress, there is a pressing need to establish consistent guidelines for creating effective and user-friendly descriptions that prioritize usability over literal accuracy. To address this challenge, we introduce a new dataset comprising 1 million existing captions for Instagram images, along with a new metric called Useful Accuracy, which evaluates the usefulness of captions for a specific task. We also establish a baseline for description generation and establish a benchmark for future research in this domain.

This study investigates the energy loss functions of TaO$_x$ (x = 1, 1.33, 2) compounds, focusing on the role of local field and spin-orbit considerations in their computation. By incorporating these factors into density functional theory-based calculations using the TaO$_x$ pseudopotentials, we obtained accurate energy loss function data. Our approach involves computing the TaO$_x$ dielectric function within the framework of density functional theory using the TaO$_x$ pseudopotentials. By applying the TaO$_x$ loss function data, we obtained accurate TaO$_x$ ionization potential values, which are in good agreement with previous Ta ionization potential values.

Social media's widespread adoption has made it easier for false information to spread, with the potential for significant harm. A key influence on online misinformation dissemination is 'The Big Sort', where individuals increasingly associate with like-minded people and become isolated from opposing viewpoints. This research aims to understand how 'The Big Sort' affects the speed at which misinformation spreads within different geographic regions. Using a combination of a large-scale agent-based simulation and real-world data from Twitter, Facebook, and the 2016 US Presidential Election, this study found that online interactions can counteract the impact of 'The Big Sort' on misinformation dissemination. Specifically, it was discovered that social media usage accelerates the spread of false information between different geographic regions by up to 50%. Furthermore, this study highlights the importance of considering online interactions when modeling the dissemination of misinformation.

Recent breakthroughs in machine learning have transformed the industry, yet they often require substantial computational resources and annotated data sets. In contrast, our proposed approach using open-ended questioning enables a novel paradigm of interaction with conversational agents. By leveraging basic feedback, the system can effectively learn and provide relevant information in various contexts. Through a series of controlled experiments, our approach has been shown to outperform traditional methods with minimal data, allowing for seamless integration into everyday devices.

Understanding the wide range of teaching methods used by humans is a key aspect of the broader challenge of learning from examples provided by people. To investigate this aspect of the problem, we analyzed a large dataset consisting of 1500 instructional videos where participants taught a virtual agent how to play a music game through spoken directions. These directions were often unclear and varied greatly in their specificity. Our findings show that the concepts expressed in the instructions are closely related to the method of demonstration, the sounds made during the process, the specific sub-tasks involved, and the mistakes made. This interdependence between these factors makes it difficult to improve the instructions simply by encouraging the teacher to make the same noises or demonstrate the same actions. We believe that the diverse examples of demonstrations and often unclear language used in the data are beneficial for developing robust teaching methods that can handle the wide range of ways people teach each other.

Researchers have long studied the central identification problem in ordered trees, focusing on the minimum number of local node properties required to uniquely identify a tree's structure. A significant breakthrough by Chvatalova in 1971 introduced the concept of distinguishing degrees, where each node's unique position in the tree is determined by its outdegree. However, this approach was limited to outdegrees only. In this paper, we introduce a new algorithm that extends this idea by incorporating multiple degree specifications - counting both incoming and outgoing connections per node. Notably, our method achieves a near-optimal degree specification, with the sum of required degrees being at most 2 less than four times the number of local node properties identified by Brodsky in 1979.

Using the Batalin-Vilkovisky formalism, we derive evolution equations for the generating functional of Green's functions in quantum field theories on a family of manifolds parameterized by t. Within the Batalin-Vilkovisky framework, we find that the BV formalism can be applied to establish that certain Euler-Arnold equations possess global solutions and are well-behaved. As a result, we prove that the given problem has solutions to a specific type of Hamilton-Jacelli-Beltrami equation and has global trajectories for the associated geodesic flow.

A significant challenge in developing conversational systems is ensuring their reliability through the use of automated testing frameworks. These frameworks are essential for the early stages of project development, yet they can be costly and complicated to implement. To address this issue, a group of researchers has created a new set of tools called HamKing, a testing framework specifically designed for the command-knowledge conversation mode. To assess HamKing's effectiveness, a group of researchers has conducted a study with 20 participants who performed a set of tasks on a mock flight booking website using a system that utilized HamKing. The results showed that the participants were able to complete the tasks successfully, with a high level of accuracy and a low error rate.

A previously unknown object with a mass similar to Earth could significantly impact future space missions to the outer solar system due to its gravity. To find such an object, we need to locate it within a certain distance, about 150 million kilometers, in most directions. Alternatively, a more massive object could be located further away, up to 600 million kilometers, in most directions. Using the N-body integrator, we simulated the object's gravitational influence on the solar system and found that it would alter the positions of planets by less than 10 kilometers. However, it could shift the positions of outer solar system bodies by up to 100 kilometers. Moreover, it could shift the positions of spacecraft, such as New Horizons, by up to 100 kilometers. Therefore, such objects are detectable through spacecraft tracking data, but they are unlikely to be found using current planetary ephemerides data. Nevertheless, they could be found by analyzing outer solar system bodies' ranging data, such as Mars orbiters, and by analyzing spacecraft tracking data, such as New Horizons' flyby.

Bilingual translation memory (TM) is a well-established and commonly used method for machine translation that achieves high precision but suffers from low recall due to reliance on near-exact source text matches. To overcome this limitation, researchers have explored various techniques to expand translation memory's recall, including multilingual TM, sparse retrieval-based methods, and translation memory augmentation. However, existing approaches either require substantial computational resources or fail to deliver significant recall improvements. In response, we introduce a Cross-lingual Translation Memory (CTM) framework, which integrates a translation memory retriever with a compact machine translation model. The CTM framework is composed of two key components: a compact and efficient memory retriever, which is trained via contrastive learning to locate relevant translations in a multi-lingual memory bank, and a compact machine translation model, which leverages retrieved memories to translate source texts. Our experiments on the IWSLT 2019 evaluation benchmark demonstrate that the CTM framework surpasses standard bilingual TM and generates translations of near-human quality with near-native accuracy. Notably, the CTM framework utilizes a single memory retriever for all target languages, requiring minimal computational resources, and achieves superior results compared to separate CTM models for each target language.

The Planck satellite's observations of the Cosmic Microwave Background revealed several unexplained irregularities, sparking renewed interest in their possible implications for the theory of cosmic inflation. A key question is whether these anomalies could arise from primordial sources, such as non-Gaussian fluctuations or variations in the universe's expansion rate. Researchers have previously searched for specific patterns, including "Hawking points" and low-variance circles, which would be evidence of such inhomogeneities. By combining the latest data from the Planck mission with more sensitive observations from ACT and SPT, a team of scientists was able to determine the likelihood of these patterns existing in the CMB. While the search yielded no conclusive results, the findings suggest that the distribution of temperature fluctuations in the CMB is consistent with the standard model, and that any evidence of inhomogeneities is minimal. Nevertheless, the search for primordial patterns in the CMB is an important one, as it could provide crucial insights into the early universe and its ultimate fate.

A study is presented that demonstrates the existence of global singular solutions for the Yamabe flow on a noncompact manifold within a short time frame, specifically when the initial condition is a compact scalar function that possesses a high degree of smoothness but is not bounded. Furthermore, given an arbitrary bounded function as an initial condition, the research shows that corresponding global singular solutions always exist. These findings were originally presented at the 10th Mathematical Sciences Summer School held in 2019.

This research introduces a novel framework for few-shot learning that focuses on robust meta-learning by dynamically identifying and eliminating ineffective meta-gradients and outlier samples from the support set. A prototype-based outlier detector is employed to recognize ineffective meta-gradients and outlier samples, with the ineffective meta-gradients being eliminated through a proposed method called Gradient Rejection, and the impact of outlier samples being mitigated by a prototype reweighting method. Experimental results on standard miniImageNet and tieredImageNet benchmarks demonstrate the superiority of our framework over existing methods in few-shot learning tasks.

In recent years, the open source community has seen a surge in self-supervised preference learning methods for recommendation systems, which have significantly outperformed traditional closed-source approaches. However, the limited availability of real-world user preference data has hindered the full potential of these methods. To bridge this gap, we introduce Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE), a novel aspect-aware preference learning framework that leverages abundant general user interactions to extract item aspects and enhance targeted preferences. GAPE employs the Dual Attention Aggregation Network (DAAN) to efficiently model user history and incorporate aspect-related information from open-source interactions. Extensive experiments across multiple real-world datasets demonstrate that GAPE significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods, particularly in scenarios with scarce targeted preference data.

In this research, various types of natural formulations using exotic cones are analyzed to understand their differences from standard formulations using conventional cones. These unusual cone formulations are examined in relation to problems involving matrix factorization, specifically matrix rank, positive semidefinite rank, and nonnegative rank. The results reveal that some of these formulations have a significantly smaller dimension compared to their conventional counterparts, particularly for matrix rank and positive semidefinite rank problems. Notably, specific instances are provided where the unusual cone formulations have a finite gap, resulting in a substantial reduction in dimensionality. The research also provides reformulations of some recent results and provides multiple examples of matrix factorization problems where the unusual cone formulations offer a significantly smaller rank than their counterparts, particularly for matrix rank and positive semidefinite rank problems. The findings suggest that some of these unusual formulations may offer a more accurate representation of certain matrix factorization problems, particularly for the matrix rank problem using the exponential cone formulation. The research also provides implications for understanding the limitations of certain reformulations and the potential benefits of exploring alternative reformulations that utilize unconventional cones.

The success of machine learning heavily relies on the data used for training. Evaluating the impact of data composition on model performance is crucial, especially when models are tested on previously unseen data. This study assesses the influence of training data on the evaluation of brain MRI segmentation models using open-access datasets. Five deep learning models were trained and tested on the OASIS-1 dataset with varying subsets of ADNI-1 and AAL1 datasets. The results showed that model performance varied significantly based on the training data used. Two types of data mismatch were identified: domain shift, where data follows the same distribution, and concept shift, where data follows a different distribution. Evaluations were conducted on models trained on both types of data mismatches using a total of 10 datasets. The experiments revealed that models trained on data with a domain shift outperformed those trained on data with a concept shift. The variation in model performance was quantified using a performance variance metric, which was found to be 10.5% for domain shift and 14.5% for concept shift. The outcome of this study highlights the importance of data composition in model performance, which has implications for the design of machine learning pipelines, including data collection, preprocessing, and model evaluation.

This paper introduces a unified analytical framework for network-based optimization problems that encompasses a range of applications, including convex optimization, stochastic communication networks, and dynamic weighted undirected graphs. Within this framework, we define and analyze the convergence properties of a distributed dual subgradient method, which incorporates local and neighbor information to update solution estimates. Our theoretical approach involves transforming the original framework into an equivalent dynamic system, which facilitates the derivation of convergence rate bounds for a variety of network-based optimization problems, including those with non-smooth objectives, time-varying objectives, and directed communication networks. Our results provide a flexible tool for assessing the performance of specific algorithms designed for these types of problems.

High-performance file systems typically rely on complex file allocation methods, which can slow down small writes. In contrast, using Optane DC Persistent Memory Modules (PMMs) allows for a significantly simpler approach. By taking advantage of Optane DC PMMs' durability, we developed a much-simplified file system called NOVA in relaxed mode, called NOVA-r. Our sledgehammer test revealed that replacing Redis with NOVA-r improved the performance of four applications by up to 2.5x for small writes, with a notable 1.9x improvement seen in the Chord DHT. Furthermore, NOVA-r outperformed the default Optane DC PMM file system by 1.5x in small write scenarios. We also created a more aggressive version of NOVA, called NOVA in strict mode, which resulted in comparable performance to using an in-memory database. Finally, NOVA in all modes produced no data corruption and a complete recovery of the file system after power outages.

The motivation behind this study is to expand the multi-agent motivation dynamics framework introduced in previous research to better capture social behaviors like rendezvous in situations involving multiple agents. To achieve this, we first generalize the original agent-based dynamics model to accommodate multiple agents, and then specifically apply this framework to rendezvous scenarios. Our model incorporates distinct motivations for different types of agents, including leaders, followers, and those who may try to separate, and successfully captures both simple and complex cooperative behaviors observed in real-world situations.

Our study focuses on the combined effects of magnetism and electronic properties in the family of $R_xM_{1-x}Sn_3$ compounds, specifically Gd$_x$Cm$_{1-x} $Sn$_3$.  Single crystals of Gd$_x$Cm$_{1-x}$Sn$_3$ were synthesized and their physical properties were thoroughly investigated.  The results from specific heat, magnetization, and Hall effect measurements were analyzed to gain a deeper understanding of the interplay between localized $4f$ electrons and itinerant electrons.  The research found that the magnetic moment of Gd$_x$Cm$_{1-x}$Sn$_3$ gradually decreases as Cm content increases, with a notable shift in magnetic anisotropy from the Gd-rich samples to Cm-rich samples.  The Gd$_x$Cm$_x$Sn$_3$ compounds exhibit a parabolic temperature dependence in the Hall coefficient, which is attributed to the interaction between the conduction electrons and the localized $4f$ electrons.  The research also found that the Hall coefficient is directly proportional to the Gd concentration, which suggests the presence of strong Kondo scattering in the Gd$_x$Cm$_{1-x}$Sn$_3$ compounds.

Within Quantum Chromodynamics, the interaction between quarks is mediated by the exchange of gluons, leading to the formation of quark-antiquark pairs known as mesons. As a consequence of their large mass, heavy quarks undergo non-relativistic motion, allowing their dynamics to be accurately described by a relativistic version of Schrödinger's equation. Over time, researchers have developed various approximations for quark-antiquark potential, yet recent advances in lattice QCD simulations have provided precise calculations of this potential. In this study, we employ a new high-accuracy lattice QCD potential to investigate the characteristics of charmonium states using first-principles methods.

Using the method of exchange pairs, we extend the study of generalized patterns (N. Reading) to osigned Coxeter groups of the classical type, specifically the 'Bn' group. Our analysis focuses on the 'Bn' group and its 'A_{n-1}' subgroups, redefining the redefined descent set to include pairs of positive indices with a negative sign. Our definition of the exchange law allows us to demonstrate that certain standardized O-signed words correspond to subwords within the original word, particularly for sets of descent that are subsets of the original set. This result is established by combining the results of previous studies on the 'Sn', 'An', and 'Dn' groups with a redefined exchange law.

We have established a comprehensive set of analytical expressions that accurately capture the radial behavior of dark matter halo profiles across their entirety. By applying these refined models to a wide range of halos, we have successfully constrained key properties including mass, scale radius, inner and outer power laws, as well as the locations of any potential breaks or steepening regions within the halo profiles. Using these profile parameters, we have calculated the gravitational potential, circular velocity, and relativistic effects within and around dark matter halos. Our profile parameters are made available to the public for future reference. In a separate study, we have examined the impact of these halo profiles on gravitational lensing, demonstrating the significance of accurate profile modeling in predicting observable effects such as Einstein radii and magnification factors.

This paper presents a novel approach to developing an abstract Hida-Watanabe theory within specific fractional Sobolev spaces, specifically those with parameter $\lambda \in (0,1)$, for the stochastic area process.

The discovery of a single T centre in 6H-SiC in 2017 was a significant milestone, as it revealed long-lived spin coherence at room temperature. Despite this breakthrough, the characteristic optical spectral diffusion observed in T centre ensembles poses a challenge for their application in solid-state quantum technologies. To address this issue, we have conducted an in-depth investigation of the optical coherence properties of the T centre using time-resolved spectroscopy techniques. By combining spatially and temporally resolved measurements, we have been able to establish a correlation between the spin state of the T centre and its corresponding optical emission. The results indicate that the spin state of the T centre undergoes rapid fluctuations, occurring on a timescale of approximately 100 picoseconds. Theoretical modelling of the T centre's structure and its interaction with the silicon valence band has provided valuable insights into the observed dynamics. The findings presented here have implications for optimizing the performance of T centre ensembles, which could be achieved through tailored stress conditions and magnetic fields.

This paper proposes a novel approach to tumor identification in medical images, combining Morphological Tools and the Region Growing Technique. Individual methods have limitations, such as Morphological Tools' sensitivity to image quality and Region Growing Technique's susceptibility to noise. By integrating both methods, we achieved enhanced tumor detection accuracy. Our results demonstrate superior performance compared to using either method alone, as validated through experiments on binary images. Findings indicate that the hybrid method yields more precise tumor detection outcomes. Further research will focus on applying this method to color images to enhance tumor detection capabilities.

This paper introduces degenerate Bernoulli numbers and polynomials, establishing their generating function and exploring their properties in relation to degenerate Stirling numbers of both kinds. It also investigates the degenerate Bernoulli numbers' connections with Circulant matrices over Galois fields and demonstrates their expressibility through degenerate Stirling numbers of both kinds.

To minimize radial velocity (RV) instability caused by spectral line noise, a new approach to choosing spectral line sets is proposed. Unlike the previous method of selecting sets based on their ability to reduce RV variability, this new approach uses either a predefined or randomly determined number of spectral lines per set. Specifically, we examine a method where sets are created by randomly selecting a certain number of lines from a specified region of a spectrum. By doing so, we can create multiple sets with different line counts, without needing a complex selection process. When testing this method using high-quality spectra of the star 55 Canorae, we found that the randomized approach yields a level of RV instability comparable to the previously used method, but with greater simplicity. Furthermore, this approach can be applied to lower-quality spectra, which were beyond the scope of our study.

This paper presents a new protocol for low-power wireless sensor networks, called HRS, which organizes nodes into hierarchical sectors using a flat positioning system. By assigning random priority levels to nodes and applying the Earliest-Transmission-First policy, HRS minimizes coordination overhead and effectively reduces network latency. Furthermore, HRS utilizes a technique called Hierarchical Range Sectoring to mitigate the hidden terminal problem by selectively activating shorter-range transmissions. As a result, HRS significantly reduces coordination overhead and achieves optimal scalability in large networks. Through extensive simulations and real-world testing, HRS has been shown to achieve optimal scalability and achieve nearly 5x better optimal scalability than existing protocols. HRS has been shown to achieve optimal scalability and achieve nearly 5x better optimal scalability than existing protocols. Hrs has been shown to achieve optimal scalability and achieve nearly 5x better optimal scalability than existing protocols.

The rise of deep learning has led to the development of numerous state-of-the-art object detectors. Due to the vast array of options available, selecting the most suitable detector can be a daunting task. To address this challenge, we introduce a unified framework that integrates nine leading object detectors into a single system. This object detection platform allows for the seamless incorporation of new detectors and provides experimenters with a standardized interface for testing multiple options. Our framework has been optimized for performance, utilizing the Intel oneDNN library and Intel Xeon CPUs to achieve a significant speedup of up to 10x compared to the native implementations of some detectors. To showcase the versatility of our framework, we have integrated it into the Disco dataset, a large-scale dataset for scene text detection. The object detection platform has been made openly available to the research community at https://github.com/oneapi-ai/Adaptivedet.

This paper addresses key questions regarding the local solvability of certain classes of degenerate and singular elliptic boundary value problems in R^n for n≥2. Specifically, we examine the equation div (|x'|^a ∇u) = λ f_i(x, u) for 1 ≤ i ≤ k, where λ ∈ R, x' represents the last k coordinates of x ∈ R^n, and 0 ≤ a < 1. To answer these questions, we employ a novel application of a local degree theory for continuous functions developed by Amann.

This study derives precise upper bounds on the expected values of functions of independent random variables under specific conditioning. Notable applications include the calculation of conditional moments of independent Bernoulli random variables, where sharp concentration results for convex functions and polynomials are obtained, along with precise alternative proofs of some of Poincaré's findings.

This letter presents an equality that equates a specific aspect of crystalline cohomology (torsion-cohomology) of a scheme over Witt vectors to an equation involving étale cohomology (also in terms of torsion-cohomology), inspired by a conjecture from Bertolini and Raskin. Firstly, we establish the compatibility of our main formula with the semicontinuity principle for étale cohomology. Secondly, we demonstrate the validity of our primary equality for smooth schemes defined over finite fields of p-power.

This study investigates the impact of the $\cos\theta_R$ asymmetry in $e^+e^-$ annihilation on the ability to measure the dihadron fragmentation function (DiFF). We find that regardless of the choice of final state cuts, the $\cos\cos\theta_R$ asymmetry remains largely unaffected by variations in event selection. Furthermore, we demonstrate that at leading twist, the $\cos\theta_R$ asymmetry provides a direct measure of the diagonal pretzelosity DiFF, while at higher twist, it offers the first opportunity to probe the pretzelosity DiFF.

In our work, we've established a transformation from de Sitter spacetime's unitary irreducible highest weight series to the general GL(2,C) Bourbaki spacetime's corresponding series. This transformation preserves invariant properties, and we've found that a specific quantity, representing Fock spacetime's path length, remains unchanged through this transformation. Interestingly, this quantity relates directly to the curvature of Bourbaki spacetime, and in cases where this quantity is very large, the curvature approaches zero, making the spacetime behave like de Sitter spacetime. Our approach is rooted in the study of global analytic functions, and we've found that the Bourbaki spacetime can be understood as a collection of de Sitter spacetime-like structures, all sharing the same fundamental quantity, and thus, they can be seen as being interconnected.

The Lie algebra of type C, corresponding to the symplectic group Sp(2n,R), consists of the symplectic matrices that adhere to the condition X = -X^T. This paper's objective is to explain the process of classifying conjugacy classes within the symplectic group, denoted as Sp(n), by identifying their distinct characteristics. Two forms, a Jordan normal form and a Williamson normal form, are central to the classification process. To facilitate a unified classification, we propose two approaches: an algorithm that combines invariants from the general linear group, GL(n), with additional data specific to the symplectic group, Sp(n), and an inductive classification method based on the partition of the symplectic group.

To improve node representations in graph-based recommendation systems, we propose a novel approach called TopoRec. TopoRec incorporates a unique perspective by modeling graph structure through the entity-relationship content, which not only captures content information but also entity-based connections. By fusing the content and topological representations, TopoRec achieves state-of-the-art performance in recommendation tasks. Our approach demonstrates significant gains in recommendation accuracy through entity representations that reflect both content and topological information.

In end-stage kidney disease, the decision to accept a blood type incompatible kidney from a deceased donor is a critical choice that directly affects patient survival. To make an informed decision, we must consider how this decision influences future health outcomes. This decision-making process can be modeled using a Markov Decision Process, with incompatible state as a key factor. However, incorporating this state variable significantly complicates the model's analysis. We propose a simplified approach that reduces the model's state space, making it easier to analyze. This approach is validated through numerical experiments and maintains accuracy comparable to the original model. Our method is user-friendly and can be easily implemented in practical settings.

Boresev and Kudryavtsev (2019) explored the use of Bayesian methods for estimating copula parameters within the framework of type I hierarchical linear models, focusing on Gaussian copula models. This paper extends that research by examining Bayesian estimation under Frank copula models, also accounting for potential right-censored data.

Recent studies highlight the use of word2vec for enhancing pre-trained language models, yet there's a lack of research on embedding quality. Our work focuses on evaluating the 2D frequency-based technique's impact on pre-trained models, particularly in the financial domain. Our experiments on three tasks - sentiment analysis, antonym recognition, and synonym recognition - using the MIT-News dataset, revealed that the frequency-based method degrades the performance of the baseline model, especially in antonym recognition. We further demonstrate that this method disproportionately affects the representation of financial terms, resulting in distorted semantic relationships. Our findings suggest that the 2D technique's over-rewarding of common terms and under-rewarding of rare terms leads to a skewed distribution, ultimately harming the models' performance.

This research focuses on enhancing secure communication between a waveforming
transmitter and a monostatic radar receiver in the presence of an eavesdropper.
By tailoring the waveform, we aim to balance the radar performance, secure
transmission, and prevent the eavesdropper from learning any information. We
propose two methods to form these waveforms and analyze their effectiveness. In
our first method, we use convex optimization to achieve fair performance among
the users, while the second method employs successive convex approximation to
find the best solution. Our numerical results show that our proposed methods can
significantly improve the secure communication performance without compromising
the radar performance, and that forming these waveforms is a non-convex problem
that requires advanced techniques to solve.

A new approach for real-time simulation of Rayleigh-Benard instability is presented, based on an adaptive spectral method. By linearizing the Navier-Stokes equations around a known stable equilibrium, our method leverages the adaptability of Lagrangian coordinates to efficiently handle the nonlinearity inherent in Lagrangian Euler coordinates. We've achieved a significant improvement in computational performance, with our adaptive scheme being $O(N\log N)$ faster than traditional spectral methods for measuring heat flux in the coordinate transformation. We've also developed an optimized matrix inversion technique that reduces the $O(N^3)$ complexity to $O(N^2)$, resulting in up to tenfold performance gains.

Noam Chomsky's generative grammar theory suggests that humans can generate infinite sentences from basic linguistic components, despite infinite potential interpretations for any given sentence. To address the problem of ambiguity in derivation, our proposed interpretation method leverages graph isomorphism to map surface forms back to their underlying grammatical structures. By utilizing the canonical labeling algorithm, this method filters out irrelevant differences and resolves the issue of infinite variability. We believe this approach offers a novel solution to understanding the generative capacity of languages.

Effective collaborative learning among multiple agents in complex cooperative tasks is crucial for the widespread adoption of multiagent reinforcement learning. One significant challenge that arises is the frequent occurrence of learning agents repeatedly taking suboptimal actions, which can hinder the overall progress. To tackle this issue, we propose a new method called CoQLEARN, a policy gradient-based method that integrates the concept of decision-theoretic utility to facilitate efficient cooperative learning. CoQLEARN allows agents to evaluate the long-term consequences of their actions, thereby reducing the frequency of suboptimal behavior. Through comprehensive experiments conducted in the Starcraft II Battle for Supremacy environment, we demonstrate the effectiveness of CoQLEARN in comparison to other learning methods, highlighting its ability to consistently avoid iteratively dominated actions and achieve better performance.

In certain contexts, resolving the balance between short-range interactions and long-distance influences in rewired networks proves crucial. We investigate whether a similar sensitivity to rewiring effects emerges in dynamic processes on such networks. We examine the impact of rewiring on the connectivity patterns resulting from a contagion process that spreads on random networks. We use the Susceptible-Infected model as an example to study this phenomenon. We find that minor rewiring changes can significantly influence the proportion of infected individuals that remain in the system at a given probability threshold $p$. We demonstrate that this sensitivity to rewiring has a more pronounced effect on $p$ in random networks than it does in complete networks. We also show that this sensitivity arises due to the formation of large, highly interconnected clusters of infected individuals. We further prove that this result holds for a process that mimics the transmission of diseases, as represented by the Susceptible-Infected model.

This paper investigates a specific type of geometry, namely, the SU(2) type, on 3-dimensional non-flat manifolds that admit a reaper field, focusing on the condition where a corresponding reaper field is orthogonal to the Reeb field. In this scenario, it is demonstrated that the geometry is locally equivalent to a warped product of a hyperbolic plane and a disk, defined as H^(-1)(t^2) x E^(1/2)(t). Moreover, this study reveals that a steady Cotton soliton exists on this type of geometry if and only if a specific parameter value is met, namely, c = -1/4. Additionally, this paper provides examples of warped product solvmanifolds that possess SU(2) type geometry and a steady Cotton-Yamabe soliton.

This paper proposes a novel methodology for fitting Parton Distribution Functions (PDFs) that inherently incorporates DGLAP evolution into the fitting process. The method employs an explicit parametric description of the PDFs at a specific initial scale, and then utilizes the discretized DGLAP equation to determine the PDFs at all other scales. Consequently, the PDF parameters can be directly fitted to experimental data, thereby eliminating the necessity for external input of the strong coupling constant $\alpha_s$, the PDF uncertainties, and the PDF plus/minus variations. Furthermore, this method allows for a straightforward calculation of the PDF and its associated uncertainties within the context of a global fit, by statistically incorporating variations in the PDF and $\alpha_s$ into the fit itself.
